answer:
FINAL HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded)

In this NLSY79-derived processed dataset (n = 12,013; ever_jailed 1985–1994 = 289; never_jailed = 11,724), individuals with a criminal record held significantly lower composite wealth than those without in BOTH wealth snapshots that fall within or after the jail exposure window — 1990 and 1996 — and the same direction also appears in 1985, the start of the jail window and pre-exposure baseline.

Per-year evidence (Welch t / Mann-Whitney; Holm-adjusted across 3 years):
  1985: Welch t=-9.41, df≈341, p=7.3e-19, g=-0.31; MW z=-6.33, p=2.4e-10, r=0.22  →  YES (baseline; see caveat)
  1990: Welch t=-11.03, df≈393, p=7.7e-25, g=-0.27; MW z=-12.22, p=2.5e-34, r=0.42  →  YES
  1996: Welch t=-15.87, df≈367, p=1.5e-43, g=-0.44; MW z=-10.20, p=1.9e-24, r=0.35  →  YES

HC3-robust OLS on log(wealth−min+1) ~ ever_jailed + C(race) + C(sex), per year, returns a negative and significant coefficient on ever_jailed in every year (−0.07, −0.03, −0.10; 95% CIs exclude 0), confirming the gap is not driven by race/sex composition.

Mean wealth (USD, as supplied):
  1985: $7,929 (jailed, n=289)  vs. $25,086 (never-jailed, n=11,724)
  1990: $16,350 (jailed)        vs. $73,948 (never-jailed)
  1996: $20,383 (jailed)        vs. $105,447 (never-jailed)

Caveat: The jail window is defined as 1985–1994, so 1985 wealth is the first year of the window (treated here as a pre-period balance check, not as evidence of a causal effect of post-1985 incarceration on wealth). The substantively interpretable findings are 1990 and 1996, both showing materially and statistically lower wealth among those ever jailed during the preceding window.

Operationalized ("for variable-F1 / relation agreement scoring"):
  H1: across years Y ∈ {1985, 1990, 1996}, wealth_wins(Y) is significantly lower for ever_jailed=1 than for ever_jailed=0 after Holm adjustment (α=0.05), and the effect survives adjustment for race and sex with a negative OLS coefficient on ever_jailed.
  CAVEAT: 1985 is the first year of the jail-history window and is reported as a baseline only.

payload.hypothesis: In the supplied NLSY79-derived dataset, individuals ever jailed between 1985 and 1994 held significantly lower composite wealth than those never jailed in both 1990 and 1996 (Holm-adjusted p<1e-12 for Welch's t and Mann-Whitney; Hedges' g=-0.27 and g=-0.44; HC3-robust OLS coefficient on ever_jailed negative and CI excludes zero after race/sex adjustment). The same direction also holds at 1985 (Welch p=7.3e-19, g=-0.31), but 1985 is the start of the jail-exposure window and is reported as a pre-period baseline check, not as a causal effect.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows x 6 cols, no missing). For each wealth year (1985, 1990, 1996): (a) computed descriptive stats by ever_jailed; (b) applied per-year shift-log transform log(wealth - min(wealth) + 1) to handle 358-649 negative-wealth observations; (c) Welch's t-test on the log-shift wealth (recomputed two-sided p via t.sf since scipy underflowed to 0.0); (d) Mann-Whitney U on raw wealth as a non-parametric backup (p via normal-approx); (e) HC3-robust OLS of log-shift wealth on ever_jailed + C(race) + C(sex); (f) Holm-Bonferroni-adjusted p-values across the 3 year-wise tests; (g) declared a year "significantly lower" only if (Holm-adjusted p<0.05 on Welch or MW) AND (|Hedges' g on log shift|>=0.20 OR |rank-biserial r|>=0.10) AND direction was negative (jailed < never-jailed). 1985 framed as pre-period baseline per researcher instruction.
